“‘What? You dig out fuller’s-earth inside the house?’
“‘No, no. We only compress it here. But that is beside the point. We simply need you to examine the machine and tell us what has gone wrong.’

“We climbed the stairs, the colonel leading with the lamp and the stout manager following with me. The old house was a maze of corridors, passages, narrow spiral stairs, and small low doors with thresholds worn hollow by generations of feet. Upstairs there were no carpets or visible furnishings. The plaster was peeling away from the walls, where damp showed in sickly green patches. I tried to maintain an air of complete unconcern. Though I had ignored the woman’s warning, I had not forgotten it, and watched both men closely. Ferguson seemed surly and taciturn. From his few remarks, however, I could tell he was at least a fellow Englishman.
“Eventually Colonel Stark stopped at a low door and unlocked it. Beyond lay a little square chamber barely large enough for the three of us. Ferguson stayed outside while the colonel showed me in.

“‘We are actually standing inside the hydraulic press,’ he explained. ‘It would be most unpleasant if someone started it now. This chamber’s ceiling is the bottom of the piston, which descends onto the metal floor with a force of many tons. Outside are small lateral columns of water which receive, transmit, and multiply the force in the way you understand. The machinery starts and runs readily enough, but its action has become stiff and it has lost some power. Perhaps you would be good enough to inspect it and show us how to correct the fault?’

“I took the lamp from him and made a very thorough examination of the machinery. It was enormous, capable of tremendous pressure. Stepping outside, I lowered its control levers. The resulting swishing immediately told me that a small leak allowed water to flow back through one side cylinder. When I examined it more closely I found that an india-rubber band around the head of a driving rod had shrunk, leaving it too small to fill the socket in which it moved. That clearly explained the loss of power. I pointed it out, and the men listened carefully, asking several practical questions about the repair. Once I had made the explanation clear to them, I returned to the main chamber for another look, simply in order to satisfy my own curiosity about it. At a glance, the fuller’s-earth explanation was plainly false. Such a powerful engine would be absurdly excessive for that purpose. Wooden walls enclosed a floor formed by a great iron trough. Inspecting it, I noticed a crust of metallic deposits covering the surface. I bent down and began scraping some away to identify it. At that moment I heard a muttered German exclamation and looked up to see the colonel’s corpse-like face above me.
“‘What are you doing?’ he demanded.

“I was angry at having been deceived by the elaborate story he had told me. ‘I was admiring your fuller’s-earth,’ I replied. ‘I think I could give you better advice about this machine if I knew the exact purpose for which you use it.’
“The moment I said it, I regretted my recklessness. His face hardened, and a murderous light appeared in his grey eyes.

“‘Very well,’ he said. ‘You shall learn everything about it.’ He stepped back, slammed the little door, and locked it. I rushed towards the door and pulled hard at its handle, but the door held firm against every kick and shove. ‘Hello!’ I shouted. ‘Hello! Colonel! Let me out!’

“Then a sound broke the silence that made my heart leap in terror: the clank of the levers and the swish of the leaking cylinder. He had started the press. My lamp remained on the floor where I had set it to examine the trough. In its light I saw the black ceiling descending, slowly and unevenly. Nobody knew better than I that within a minute its force would crush me into an unrecognisable mass. Screaming, I hurled myself against the door and clawed at the lock. I begged the colonel to release me, but the relentless machinery drowned my cries. The ceiling was now only a foot or two above my head. Raising my hand, I could feel its hard, rough underside. Suddenly I realised that the pain of dying would depend largely on my position. Face down, I would receive the weight on my spine. I shuddered at the thought of that dreadful crack. Perhaps lying on my back would be easier—but could I bear to watch the deadly black shadow wavering down towards me? Already I could no longer stand upright. Then I saw something that sent hope flooding back.

“As I said, though the floor and ceiling were iron, the walls were wooden. One last desperate glance revealed a thin yellow line between two boards. It widened as a small panel slid back. For an instant I could scarcely believe this really was a doorway away from death. The next moment I flung myself through it and lay half fainting on the other side. The panel shut behind me. My lamp smashed, and a few seconds later the two iron surfaces clanged together, telling me how narrowly I had escaped.

“A frantic tug at my wrist brought me to myself. I lay on the stone floor of a narrow passage. A woman bent over me, pulling with her left hand and holding a candle in her right. It was the kind protector whose warning I had so foolishly dismissed.
“‘Come! Come!’ she gasped. ‘They will arrive in a moment. They will find you gone. Oh, do not waste precious time. Come!’

“This time, at least, I did not disregard her advice. I staggered to my feet and ran beside her down the corridor and a winding staircase. The stairs led into another broad passage. Just as we reached it, we heard running feet and two voices shouting to each other, one on our own floor and the other from below. My guide stopped and looked around, apparently at a loss for what to do. Then she threw open a door into a bedroom where bright moonlight streamed through the window.
“‘Your only chance,’ she said. ‘It is high, but perhaps you can make the jump.’

“As she spoke, a light appeared at the passage’s far end. Colonel Stark’s lean figure rushed towards us, a lantern in one hand and something like a butcher’s cleaver in the other. I ran across the bedroom, opened the window, and looked down. How peaceful, lovely, and wholesome the garden looked under the moon! The drop could be no more than thirty feet. I climbed onto the sill, but waited before jumping to hear what passed between my rescuer and the brute pursuing me. If he hurt her, I was determined to return and help, whatever the risk. Scarcely had I thought it when he reached the door and tried to push past her. She threw her arms around him, struggling to restrain him.
“‘Fritz! Fritz!’ she cried in English. ‘Remember what you promised after last time. You said it would never happen again. He will keep silent! Oh, he will!’

“‘You are mad, Elise!’ he shouted, trying to free himself. ‘You will destroy us. He knows too much. Stand aside!’ He flung her away, rushed to the window, and struck at me with the heavy blade. I had lowered myself and was hanging from the sill by my hands when the blow came. I felt a dull pain; my grip failed, and I dropped into the garden.

“The fall shook me but did not injure me. Knowing I was still far from safe, I picked myself up and ran through the bushes as fast as possible. Suddenly a terrible dizziness and nausea overcame me. I glanced down at my painfully throbbing hand and saw for the first time that my thumb was gone and blood was streaming from the wound. I tried to bind it with my handkerchief. Then a sudden buzzing filled my ears, and I collapsed unconscious among the rose bushes.

“I cannot say how long I lay unconscious, but it must have been many hours. The moon had already sunk out of sight and a bright morning was beginning when I woke. Dew soaked all my clothes, and blood from the thumb wound had drenched my coat sleeve. Its burning pain instantly brought back every detail of the night. I jumped up, afraid my pursuers might still be near. To my astonishment, however, neither house nor garden was visible. I had been lying in a corner of a hedge beside the main road. A little farther down stood a long building. As I approached, I recognised the very station at which I had arrived the previous night. Without that dreadful wound, everything I had endured might have been a nightmare.

“Still dazed, I entered the station and asked about a morning train. One would leave for Reading in less than an hour. The porter on duty was the same man who had been there when I arrived. Had he heard of Colonel Lysander Stark? He did not know the name. Had he noticed a carriage waiting for me the night before? No. Was there a police station nearby? Yes, about three miles away.

“I was too weak and ill to go so far. I decided to wait until I reached London before approaching the police. I arrived a little after six and went first to have the wound dressed. The doctor kindly brought me here afterwards. I now place the affair in your hands and will follow your advice exactly.”
For a while after this astonishing account, neither of us spoke. Then Holmes took from a shelf one of the heavy scrapbooks in which he stored newspaper cuttings.

“This advertisement will interest you,” he said. “It ran in all the papers about a year ago. Listen: ‘Missing since the ninth of this month: Mr. Jeremiah Hayling, twenty-six, hydraulic engineer. He left his lodgings at ten in the evening and has not been heard from since. He was wearing’—and so on. Ah! I suspect that was the previous occasion on which the colonel needed his machinery serviced.”
“Good heavens!” my patient cried. “Then that explains the woman’s words.”

“Certainly. The colonel is clearly cold-blooded and desperate, determined to let nothing interfere with his scheme. He is like those utterly ruthless pirates who leave nobody alive aboard a captured vessel. Every moment is precious to us now. If you feel able, let us go straight to Scotland Yard and arrange our journey to Eyford.”

About three hours later we were all aboard a train from Reading to the little Berkshire village: Holmes, the hydraulic engineer, Inspector Bradstreet of Scotland Yard, a plain-clothes officer, and I. Bradstreet spread an Ordnance map across the seat and used compasses to draw a circle centred on Eyford.
“There,” he said. “A circle with a ten-mile radius around the village. The house must be somewhere near its edge. You said ten miles, I believe, sir?”
“We drove for a good hour.”
“And you suppose they carried you that entire distance back while you were unconscious?”
“They must have. I also have a rather confused recollection of being lifted up and carried somewhere.”
“What puzzles me,” I said, “is why they spared you after finding you unconscious in the garden. Perhaps the woman’s pleas softened the villain.”
“I very much doubt it. I have never seen a more merciless face.”
“We shall soon discover all that,” Bradstreet replied. “Well, I have now drawn my circle on the map. I only wish I knew where along it to find the people we want.”
“I believe I could point to the spot,” Holmes said quietly.
“Really!” the inspector exclaimed. “You have formed an opinion already, then! Let us see who agrees. I choose south: the countryside is more deserted there.”
“I choose east,” my patient said.
“West for me,” the plain-clothes officer remarked. “There are several secluded little villages that way.”
“And I choose north,” I said. “There are no hills in that direction, and our friend noticed no climb during the drive.”
“Well!” the inspector laughed. “A fine range of opinions! Between us we have covered the compass. Who gets your deciding vote?”
“Every one of you is wrong.”
“But surely we cannot all be wrong.”
“Indeed you can. Here is my choice.” He touched the centre of the circle. “This is where we shall find them.”
“But the twelve-mile journey!” Hatherley gasped.
“Six miles out and six back. Perfectly simple. You said the horse was fresh and glossy when you entered the carriage. How could it look like that after twelve miles on bad roads?”
“A plausible trick, certainly,” Bradstreet said thoughtfully. “And of course we can have no doubt what sort of gang they are.”
“None,” Holmes replied. “They manufacture counterfeit coins on a large scale. They have used the machine to form the amalgam they substitute for silver.”

“We have known for some time that a very skilful gang was operating,” the inspector said. “They have produced half-crowns by the thousand. We tracked them as far as Reading, then lost the trail. They covered their movements like experienced hands. Thanks to this lucky accident, however, I believe we have finally caught them.”

The inspector was mistaken. These criminals were not destined to face justice. As we entered Eyford Station, we saw an enormous column of smoke rising behind a nearby cluster of trees. It hung over the countryside like a gigantic ostrich feather.
“Is a house burning?” Bradstreet asked as the train steamed away again on its journey.
“Yes, sir!” the station-master replied.
“When did the fire start?”
“During the night, I hear, sir. But it has spread, and now the whole place is ablaze.”
“Who owns the house?”
“Dr. Becher does.”
“Tell me,” the engineer interrupted, “is he a very thin German with a long, pointed nose?”

The station-master laughed heartily. “No, sir. Dr. Becher is English, and nobody in the parish fills his waistcoat better. But a foreign gentleman is staying with him, a patient, I understand. A little good Berkshire beef would do that one no harm.”

Before he had finished, we were all hurrying towards the blaze. The road climbed over the crest of a low hill. Ahead stood a large, sprawling, whitewashed house with flames pouring from every window and crevice. Three fire engines in the front garden struggled vainly to control them.
“That is the house!” Hatherley cried excitedly. “There is the gravel drive, and those are the rose bushes where I fell. I jumped from that second window.”

“At least you have taken your revenge on them,” Holmes said. “There can be no doubt that your oil lamp ignited the wooden walls when the press crushed it. They were probably too excited by the pursuit to notice the fire at the time. Now keep a careful watch on this crowd for your acquaintances of last night, though I very much fear they are a good hundred miles away already.”

His fears proved justified. From that day to this, nothing has been heard of the beautiful woman, the sinister German, or the surly Englishman. Early that morning a countryman saw a cart carrying several people and very large boxes travelling rapidly towards Reading. There the fugitives’ trail ended. Even Holmes’s ingenuity never uncovered the slightest clue to their whereabouts.

The firemen had been much disturbed by the strange arrangements they found inside the house, and still more by a freshly severed human thumb on a second-floor window sill. Around sunset their efforts finally succeeded and they managed to bring the flames under control. By then the roof had collapsed and the building was utterly ruined. Apart from twisted cylinders and iron pipes, nothing remained of the machinery that had cost our unfortunate acquaintance so dearly. An outbuilding contained large quantities of nickel and tin, but not a single coin could be found. That might explain the bulky boxes I have mentioned.

How the engineer reached the place where he regained consciousness might have remained a mystery, but the soft earth left us a very clear account of what had happened. He had evidently been carried to that spot by two people, one with remarkably small feet, the other with unusually large ones. Most likely the taciturn Englishman, either less daring or less murderous than his companion, had helped the woman take the unconscious man out of danger.
“Well,” our engineer said sadly as we sat down for the return to London, “what a fine affair for me! I have lost my thumb and a fifty-guinea fee. What have I gained?”
“Experience,” Holmes replied, laughing. “That may have an indirect value. Put it into words, and you can earn a reputation as excellent company for the rest of your life.”
